title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python?

The basic difference: R was built by statisticians for statisticians, so the focus is narrower.
Python was built by software engineers for general purpose applications, so the focus is broad.
R is great for focusing on thinking about statistical problems, solving them, and communicating the results
Python is great for doing lots of different things. Example, download thousands of YouTube videos, analyze the images frame by frame, transcribe the sound into words, analyze the data, etc.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

R is “Problem-First” or “Problem-Forward”
In R, data structures are integrated directly into the language and do not require additional tools (but tools, found in libraries, are helpful).
When you load a dataset, R assumes you want to analyze it. The syntax is designed to mirror the way a researcher thinks: “I want to study something which involves data, get the data, then filter/subset it, then group it, then summarize/describe, then model, etc.”

Also R’s simpler modeling formulas allows one to remain thinking about the analytical problem.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

Python is “System-First”
In Python, you “build” your environment before you can solve the problem (importing tools, found in libraries such as pandas, numpy, etc.)
In Python, it matters how your programming code integrates within a larger system, the result is versatility. So it is easy for Python to interact with YouTube for example (not as easy/or maybe not possible in R)
In R, what matters is how the programming code helps you reveal the truth found in the data.

title: Lecture 01
text:
The “Formula” vs. “The Matrix”
In R, a statistical model is treated like a scientific hypothesis. In Python, a statistical model is treated like “how does the computer wants its input formatted?”

R Approach: You use formulas (y ~ x). This is like saying “I think \(y\) changes in response to \(x\).” R automatically handles things creating the underlying matrix and keeps the names of your variables intact so you can read the results.
Python Approach: Most Python libraries(toolkits) require you to manually transform your data into a matrix of numbers first. Then pass them in as \(x\) and \(y\).

In R, the code looks like the math inside your head. In Python, the code looks like the way the computer understands math.

title: Lecture 01
text:
R v Python Example 2
R allows for a more linear flow of thought, less engineering, more thinking. Not good or bad, just a different philosophy. In each of these examples, we filter (subset/split up), aggregate (combine), then analyze:

RPythonPython with pandasPython one line


R uses the “pipe” operator (%>% Tidyverse library or |> core R) which is read like “then”. You know zero R today, but with a little help, you can read your R code like a sentence.
library(dplyr)                    # a library is like a toolbox filled with helpful functions
df %>%                            # df stands for "data frame", you'll learn more about this data structure soon 
  filter(year > 2020) %>%         # filter() function - keep these years in the data frame
  group_by(state) %>%             # Then, "group the data by" state for analysis
  summarize(mean_yield = mean(y)) # Finally, calculate the mean() save it to a new variable mean_yield
We created a new variable just by naming it.


In Python, you frequently create “intermediate” variables or use complex nested brackets to do the same:
from collections import defaultdict

## filter
filtered = [row for row in data if row["year"] > 2020]

## group and accumulate sums and counts
sums = defaultdict(float)
counts = defaultdict(int)

for row in filtered:
    state = row["state"]
    y = row["y"]
    sums[state] += y
    counts[state] += 1

## compute means
mean_yield_by_state = {
    state: sums[state] / counts[state]
    for state in sums
}

## print the result
for state, mean_yield in mean_yield_by_state.items():
    print(state, mean_yield)


This is why pandas exists (compare Python using pandas against the previous Python no pandas)
import pandas as pd

## assume df is a data frame in Python
result = (
    df[df["year"] > 2020]          ## Keep these years
      .groupby("state", as_index=False) ## aggregate by state  
      .agg(mean_yield=("y", "mean"))  ## Calculate the mean of y and store as mean_yield
)

print(result)

title: A note on R objects and their names
text:
from Chapter 2.2 “Binding Basics”
Consider this code:

x <- c(1, 2, 3)

It’s easy to read it as: “create an object named ‘x’, containing the values 1, 2, and 3”. ( or R object ‘x’ gets the vector 1, 2, 3 ) Unfortunately, that’s a simplification that will lead to inaccurate predictions about what R is actually doing behind the scenes. It’s more accurate to say that this code is doing two things:

It’s creating an object, a vector of values, c(1, 2, 3).
And it’s binding (associating) that object to a name, x.

In other words, the object, or value, (technically) doesn’t have a name; it’s actually the name x here that has a value 1, 2, 3.
To further clarify this distinction, I’ll draw diagrams like this:








The name, x, is drawn with a rounded rectangle. It has an arrow that points to (or binds or references) the value, the vector c(1, 2, 3). The arrow points in opposite direction to the assignment arrow: <- creates a binding from the name on the left-hand side to the object on the right-hand side.
Thus, you can think of a name as a reference to a value. For example, if you run this code, you don’t get another copy of the value c(1, 2, 3), you get another binding to the existing object:

y <- x









You might have noticed that the value c(1, 2, 3) has a label: 0x74b. While the vector doesn’t have a name, I’ll occasionally need to refer to an object independent of its bindings. To make that possible, I’ll label values with a unique identifier. These identifiers have a special form that looks like the object’s memory “address”, i.e. the location in memory where the object is stored. But because the actual memory addresses changes every time the code is run, we use these identifiers instead.
You can access an object’s identifier with lobstr::obj_addr(). Doing so allows you to see that both x and y point to the same identifier:

obj_addr(x)

[1] "0x14258d6c8"

obj_addr(y)

[1] "0x14258d6c8"


These identifiers are long, and change every time you restart R.
It can take some time to get your head around the distinction between names and values, but understanding this is really helpful in functional programming where functions can have different names in different contexts.
(end Wickham)

title: A note on R objects and their names
text:
The result of R’s ways
So take a look at what happens when we modify one but not the other

y[[3]] <- 4   ## I am following Wickham's style here, 

## instead you could have used y[3] <- 4 
## read as "y's third element" gets 4
## because we have simple vector, in other places 
## y[[3]] <- 4 is clearer, but we're not there yet

x

[1] 1 2 3

y

[1] 1 2 4


let’s check the memory locations

obj_addr(x)

[1] "0x14258d6c8"

obj_addr(y)

[1] "0x114e06f78"


(start Wickham again)
Modifying y clearly didn’t modify x. So what happened to the shared binding? While the value associated with y changed, the original object did not. Instead, R created a new object, 0xcd2, a copy of 0x74b with one value changed, then rebound y to that object.








This behaviour is called copy-on-modify. Understanding it will radically improve your intuition about the performance of R code.
(end Wickham)
Do you need to completely understand this to do well in Stats 20? Probably not BUT if you decide to learn Python or become a paid R programmer later (because all of the documentation assumes you understand R’s decision making in memory), it would help to understand what he is trying to tell you in Chapter 2 of the textbook Advanced R.

The vector
In the example of x, y and z, a numeric vector is a sequence of values that are all of the same type (in this case, numbers). In R, the vector (there are different types, later…) is the fundamental data structure.
Notice that for a single number, R still treats it as a vector of length 1 (there are no scalars in R) with index [1]. This is a common source of confusion for those new to R. R is 1-indexed, meaning enumeration starts at 1. It is like the way we count. Python, C / C++, Java, JavaScript and many other programming languages are 0-indexed, meaning enumeration starts at 0.

You can give a value a name (called a variable, like math), and then use that name (variable) in calculations and to store results.
R has many built-in data sets such as iris and rivers that you can use to practice your data manipulation and analysis skills.
Functions do all of the work in R. They have arguments that you can modify to get different results. For example, head() is a function that takes an R (typically) data object as an argument (it can take other kinds of R objects).
The is() function tells you what type of R object you are working with.
The vector is the most basic type of data object in R, and it is a sequence of values that are all of the same type.
The data frame is a more complex type of R object that consists of multiple vectors (columns) that can be of different types (numbers, factors, etc.).
R vectors are 1-indexed (numbered starting with 1), even when the vector only has one value (there are no scalars in R, only vectors).
The str() function gives you a quick overview of the structure of an R object.
The summary() function gives you a quick summary of the data in each vector (column) of a data frame.

Simplistic but useful “rule”: everything in R is an object.

An object is storage space (memory) with an associated name.
For Stats 20 an R object could be a constant, a variable, a data structure, a function (operators are functions) and they are reusable.

title: Lecture 03
text:
Names are (R?) Important

R is case sensitive so the name junk is different from JUNK or juNk.
R object names should start with a period OR a letter (and nothing else)
so .first_value is a valid R object name and if a name starts with a period, a letter should follow.
Variables and functions that you create have names with only lowercase letters, numbers, and _. Use underscores (_) (so called snake case) to separate words within a name. For example: this_is_my_first_variable <- 1:1000
While periods are legal, you may wish to avoid using them because R uses them to name its own functions and variables.
R object names can have spaces and start with periods and numbers, but these names need to be quoted with backticks to be used. So if you have a variable name like Zip Code, when you access it, you will need to call it using `Zip Code`.
The overall goal is to be understood when sharing code. So clarity, readability and following common conventions are useful. The habit of good naming hygiene is important for Stats 102ABC.

text:
The basics of functions

Functions do all of the work in R. They typically produce results.
Functions, identifiable by their name (for example class) followed by a set of parentheses ()
The values inside the parentheses are the inputs to the function
Functions are versatile and can even accept other functions as inputs
Another way to say it: when we use (call) an R function, we pass arguments inside of its parentheses.

R Vectors are the core data structure

OverviewVector ConstructionBuilt-insTakeaways



We can construct vectors, use built-in vectors, extract vectors from data structures (like a data frame) and generate vectors from other vectors and from functions
vectors contain values of the same type (AKA atomic) and allow you operate on all of the values at once
numeric, integer, character, logical, complex, factor, raw are the basic vector types
R functions typically operate on vectors and operate on their values all at once (vectorized operation)
This is not an exaggeration – all data in R can be conceptualized as being stored in a vector-like structure

Math with Vectors

OverviewSimple ExampleWarningsRecycling ExampleRecycling



R operates on entire vectors. This feature extends infinitely in every direction and it makes processing rapid.
Another name for this is vectorization, in other words, entire vectors are passed through an R function using a single call instead of calling the R function repeatedly for each element of a vector.




a12 <- 1:12
b12 <- c(6, 8, 18, 5, 7, 1, 13, 12, 4, 10, 20, 11)

a12^2

 [1]   1   4   9  16  25  36  49  64  81 100 121 144

b12 + 10

 [1] 16 18 28 15 17 11 23 22 14 20 30 21

a12 + b12 # did either original change?

 [1]  7 10 21  9 12  7 20 20 13 20 31 23

 [1]   7  12  27  21  32  37  62  76  85 110 141 155

sqrt(a12 * b12)

 [1]  2.449490  4.000000  7.348469  4.472136  5.916080  2.449490  9.539392
 [8]  9.797959  6.000000 10.000000 14.832397 11.489125





Element-wise execution in R can be treacherous because base R will perform math even when vectors differ in length (some packages prevent this from happening).
R does not issue an error when vectors differ in length, instead shorter vectors in the expression are recycled as often as needed until they match the length of the longest vector.
If the lengths of your vectors differ, the result of the expression is a vector with the same length as the longest vector which occurs in the expression.
R will only issue a warning if the longest is not a multiple of the shortest. This is neither good nor bad - just know that it happens




c4 <- c(100, 200, 300, 400)
d5 <- c(1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000)

title: Lecture 03

Coercion

Types againLogicalInt/NumLogical/CharNum/Char



Recall there are different data types, when combining types, R follows a hierarchy


Logical (TRUE/FALSE) is the lowest
Integer
Numeric (double)
Complex (probably not in Stats 20)
Character
Factor (later)
Raw (not in Stats 20) is the highest

When you combine different types of vectors, R will coerce them to the type that is higher in the hierarchy. Some functions in R behave this way – coercing data types to suit its needs.



Logical (TRUE/FALSE) occupies the bottom of the hierarchy, it’s always coerced if combined with any non-Logical type of data.


logical_vector <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
integer_vector <- 1:10 # colon operator generates integers

logical_c_integer <- c(logical_vector, integer_vector)

logical_plus_integer <- logical_vector + integer_vector # recycled too

A matrix could be thought of as a vector with row and column dimensions imposed on it
Matrices then are rectangular
Matrices, like vectors, must be a single data type (will coerce data if not)

The “Formula” vs. “The Matrix”
In R, a statistical model is treated like a scientific hypothesis. In Python, it is treated like how the computer wants its input formatted.

In R, the code looks like the math inside your head. In Python, the code looks like the way the computer understands math.

R v Python Example 2
R allows for a more linear flow of thought, less engineering, more thinking. Not good or bad, just a different philosophy. In each of these examples, we filter (subset/split up), aggregate (combine), then analyze:

RPythonPython with pandasPython one line


R uses the “pipe” operator (%>% Tidyverse library or |> core R) which is read like “then”. You know zero R today, but with a little help, you can read your R code like a sentence.
library(dplyr)                    # a library is like a toolbox filled with helpful functions
df %>%                            # df stands for "data frame", you'll learn more about this data structure soon 
  filter(year > 2020) %>%         # filter() function - keep these years in the data frame
  group_by(state) %>%             # Then, "group the data by" state for analysis
  summarize(mean_yield = mean(y)) # Finally, calculate the mean() save it to a new variable mean_yield
We created a new variable just by naming it.


In Python, you frequently create “intermediate” variables or use complex nested brackets to do the same:
from collections import defaultdict

## filter
filtered = [row for row in data if row["year"] > 2020]

## group and accumulate sums and counts
sums = defaultdict(float)
counts = defaultdict(int)

for row in filtered:
    state = row["state"]
    y = row["y"]
    sums[state] += y
    counts[state] += 1

## compute means
mean_yield_by_state = {
    state: sums[state] / counts[state]
    for state in sums
}

## print the result
for state, mean_yield in mean_yield_by_state.items():
    print(state, mean_yield)


This is why pandas exists (compare Python using pandas against the previous Python no pandas)
import pandas as pd

## assume df is a data frame in Python
result = (
    df[df["year"] > 2020]          ## Keep these years
      .groupby("state", as_index=False) ## aggregate by state  
      .agg(mean_yield=("y", "mean"))  ## Calculate the mean of y and store as mean_yield
)

Focus on what matters, minimize what does not:

defining a function that works for “any dataset”

Abstraction is what helps you generalize from one analysis to the next. This helps maximize productivity and minimize time spent in repetitive tasks.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.close("all")

import statsmodels.api as sm

mtcars = sm.datasets.get_rdataset("mtcars").data
X = sm.add_constant(mtcars["wt"])
y = mtcars["mpg"]
model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()

# 2. Setup Figure
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

# Plot the points (open circles like R)
ax.scatter(model.fittedvalues, model.resid, facecolors='none', edgecolors='black')

# Add the horizontal 'zero' line
ax.axhline(0, color='silver', linestyle=':', zorder=0)

# 3. Add the Red Lowess Line (The 'R' special)
lowess = sm.nonparametric.lowess(model.resid, model.fittedvalues, frac=2/3)
ax.plot(lowess[:, 0], lowess[:, 1], color='red', lw=1, alpha=0.8)

# 4. Label the Top 3 Outliers
# Find indices of the 3 largest absolute residuals
top_3_idx = np.abs(model.resid).sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).index

for i in top_3_idx:
    ax.annotate(i, (model.fittedvalues[i], model.resid[i]), 
                xytext=(5, 5), textcoords='offset points', fontsize=9)

# Formatting
ax.set_title("Residuals vs Fitted")
ax.set_xlabel("Fitted values")
ax.set_ylabel("Residuals")
plt.savefig("01_residuals_vs_fitted.png")
